fatal_errors: The proposed material is AlCoCrFeNi rather than the studied eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, omitting the composition and L12/B2 lamellar microstructure central to its performance.
The hypothesis replaces aqueous tribo-corrosion at 25–100 °C after rapid thermal-shock cycles with continuous testing near 600 °C in saline, a fundamentally different exposure regime.
It does not identify identically conditioned duplex stainless steel 2205 as the comparator.

The asserted protective high-temperature oxide-scale mechanism is unsupported and misses the observed competition among depassivation, repassivation, tribo-layer rupture, abrasion, and debris-assisted wear.

The proposed 600 °C saline electrochemical experiment is not operationally defined; an ordinary aqueous saline solution cannot remain liquid at that temperature without a specified high-pressure apparatus.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad proposition that an Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-family HEA may outperform conventional alloys under combined wear and corrosion, and it proposes measurable comparative outcomes. However, it fails to reconstruct the specific AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy, DS2205 baseline, thermal-shock protocol, deionized-water reciprocating tests, and nonmonotonic temperature response with minimum degradation near 50 °C. Its generic self-healing oxide explanation only weakly overlaps with passivation and tribo-layer repair and ignores phase retention and temperature-dependent wear-mode transitions. With no cited evidence and a poorly defined 600 °C saline experiment, the alternative remains unsupported rather than a well-substantiated plausible reconstruction.
